lead: Today we keep the memory of Mar Aprem Malpan, St Ephrem the Syrian, the poet of our Syriac tradition, who loved to find Christ foreshadowed throughout the Scriptures. The Epistle fits him well: the law has “only a shadow of the good things to come”. In the Gospel Jesus shows us the reality behind every shadow: love that lays down its life for friends. “I have called you friends.” The key words are shadow and friendship.

r.h: A shadow of the good things to come
set: The Letter to the Hebrews does not name its author. Ancient tradition linked it with Paul, but already in the third century Origen said that only God knows who wrote it. It is a long sermon to Christians tempted to grow tired in faith, and its centre is Christ the high priest. In chapters 8–10 the author compares the sacrifices of the first covenant, above all those of the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16), with the one sacrifice of Christ. Our verses explain why the old sacrifices were repeated year after year.
str: v. 1: the law has a shadow, not the true form; its sacrifices cannot make perfect.
v. 2: if they could, they would have ceased.
v. 3: instead, they bring a yearly reminder of sin.
v. 4: the blood of bulls and goats cannot take away sins.
kw: A shadow shows the outline of something real but is not the thing itself. The eikōn is the reality in its own form. The worship of Israel was given by God and was true worship, but it pointed beyond itself to Christ.

The same word Jesus uses at the Last Supper: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19). The old sacrifices recalled sin each year; the new remembrance makes present the sacrifice that takes sin away.
vv: Since the law has only a shadow of the good things to come and not the true form of these realities,
The “good things to come” have now come in Christ. The shadow is not despised; it is honoured as the sign that the light was coming.
But in these sacrifices there is a reminder of sin year after year.
On the Day of Atonement the high priest entered the Holy of Holies once a year. The repetition itself showed that the final cleansing had not yet come.
For it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins.

The psalms and the prophets had already said that God desires mercy and a contrite heart more than sacrifice (Psalm 51:16–17; Hosea 6:6). Hebrews goes on to quote Psalm 40: “a body you have prepared for me” (10:5). The true sacrifice is the self-offering of the Son.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the priesthood of the old covenant, though instituted by God, was powerless to bring about salvation, and so needed to repeat its sacrifices without end; only Christ's sacrifice, offered once for all, achieves it (CCC 1540). The Holy Qurbono does not add new sacrifices to his. It makes present the one sacrifice of the cross, so that the sacrifice of Christ and the sacrifice of the Eucharist are one single sacrifice (CCC 1366–1367). The shadows of Israel's worship are fulfilled, not erased.

set: These words belong to the farewell discourse at the Last Supper. Jesus has just spoken of himself as the true vine and his disciples as the branches (15:1–8), and has told them, “As the Father has loved me, so I have loved you; abide in my love” (15:9). Now he explains what that love asks and gives: joy, the commandment of love, friendship, and lasting fruit.
str: v. 11: that my joy may be in you.
v. 12: the commandment: love one another as I have loved you.
v. 13: no greater love than to lay down one's life for friends.
vv. 14–15: you are my friends; I have made known everything.
vv. 16–17: I chose you to bear lasting fruit; love one another.
kw: In the Old Testament, Abraham is called God's friend (Isaiah 41:8), and the Lord spoke to Moses “face to face, as one speaks to a friend” (Exodus 33:11). Jesus now gives this title to all his disciples.
The self-giving love that seeks the good of the other. Its measure is not our feeling but “as I have loved you”: the love shown on the cross.
The key word of chapter 15. The branch remains in the vine, the disciple in Jesus' love, and the fruit lasts.
vv: This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you.
“As I have loved you” makes the commandment new (13:34). It is not only “as you love yourself” but as Christ loves: to the end.
No one has greater love than this, to lay down one's life for one's friends.
Jesus speaks these words a few hours before he lays down his own life. The commandment is preceded and made possible by his example.
but I have called you friends, because I have made known to you everything that I have heard from my Father.
A servant receives orders; a friend receives confidences. Jesus shares with his disciples what is in the Father's heart.
You did not choose me but I chose you.
Every vocation begins with Christ's choice. In rabbinic custom a disciple chose his master; here the master chooses the disciples, and sends them to bear fruit.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus makes charity the new commandment, and that by loving his own to the end he shows the Father's love which he receives; by loving one another, the disciples imitate the love of Jesus which they themselves receive (CCC 1823). The friendship of which Jesus speaks is the heart of Christian prayer and life. It is offered to every disciple, and the saints are those who accepted it without reserve.

qa: Does Hebrews say that the sacrifices of the Old Testament were worthless?

No. They were given by God, offered in obedience and faith, and they taught Israel about sin, holiness and God's mercy. Hebrews says they were a shadow, which means they were real signs of a reality still to come. The Church honours them as part of God's plan and sees in them a preparation for Christ (CCC 1540). The one who fulfils them is himself a son of Israel.
rite: Our Church keeps today the memory of Mar Aprem Malpan, St Ephrem the Syrian. He was born at Nisibis in Mesopotamia early in the fourth century, served there as a deacon and teacher, and when Nisibis was handed over to Persia in 363 he moved with many Christians to Edessa, where he died in 373. He remained a deacon all his life. His hymns, the madrāšē, taught the faith in song, and the Syriac Churches still pray with them; tradition calls him the Harp of the Spirit. In 1920 Pope Benedict XV declared him a Doctor of the Church. Ephrem loved to see in Scripture and in nature symbols that point to Christ, and he would have recognized in today's Epistle his own way of reading: the shadows of the law are true, and they lead to the Son. He is a fitting patron for the Apostles' Fast, a man of prayer and fasting who, as tradition remembers, organised help for the hungry when famine struck Edessa.
study: Hebrews calls the old sacrifices a shadow of good things to come. How does knowing the Old Testament help me understand what happens in the Holy Qurbono?
Jesus calls me his friend. What would change in my prayer if I spoke to him as a friend who has chosen me?
